Every place on Earth has a climate you can summarise in a single picture: how
warm it is each month, and how much rain falls. Putting those two curves on one
chart results in a **climate diagram** (or a Walter–Lieth diagram, after the
two ecologists who standardised it). **Click anywhere** on the map below and one
will be drawn for that spot.

## Explore

Click the map, pick a biome from the menu, or type coordinates. The link in your
browser's address bar updates as you go, so you can copy it to share or hand in
a specific location.

## Things to try

- Compare **Manaus** and **Darwin**. Both are tropical and both are hot all
  year — so why is one rainforest and the other savanna? Look at the dry season.
- Find **Nairobi**. It sits almost exactly on the equator, but it is not hot.
  Check the elevation in the diagram header.
- Click somewhere in the **Andes**, then somewhere in **Kansas**. Notice which
  diagram warns you that the grid cell is hiding a lot of terrain, and think
  about what that means for how much you should trust it.
- Walk north up a single line of longitude — say 100° W — from Mexico to the
  Arctic, clicking every few degrees. Watch the temperature curve flatten out
  and drop.

## How to read a climate diagram

::: {.cd-howto}

**Two lines, two axes.** The red line is *temperature*, read against the axis on
the **left** in °C. The blue line is *rainfall*, read against the axis on the
**right** in mm. Each point is an average for that month.

**The two axes are deliberately linked.** 10 °C on the left lines up with 20 mm
on the right. That is not an accident — it is the whole trick of the diagram.
Where the rainfall line sits *above* the temperature line, more water arrives
than the warmth can evaporate, and plants have water to work with: a **wet
season** (blue hatching). Where rainfall drops *below* temperature, it is a
**dry season** (orange dots). You can spot a Mediterranean summer drought or a
monsoon instantly, without reading a single number.

**The right-hand axis changes scale at 100 mm.** Below 100 mm each 10 °C is
20 mm; above it, each 10 °C is 200 mm. Without that squeeze, a wet tropical
month would run off the top of the page. The chart marks where the change
happens — watch for it, because it makes very wet months look flatter than they
are.

**A note on months.** Southern-hemisphere diagrams start in July, so that summer
sits in the middle of the chart just as it does for northern ones. The chart
says so when it does this.

:::

## About the data

Monthly averages come from **WorldClim 2.1**, which describes the climate of
**1970–2000** — a 30-year average, not this year's weather, and not a forecast.
Values are given for grid cells 0.5° across (roughly 55 km north–south), so each
diagram describes a *region*, not a point. In mountainous or coastal places the
real climate can vary sharply inside one cell, and the diagram says so when the
terrain warrants it.

Fick, S.E. and R.J. Hijmans (2017). WorldClim 2: new 1 km spatial resolution
climate surfaces for global land areas. *International Journal of Climatology*
37(12): 4302–4315.
